facts.fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
facts.hook: Drafting what to say to a best friend, a student crosses out 'You ditched me' and tries starting with 'I felt'.

facts.fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
facts.hook: A kid decides their friend is just selfish for skipping the sleepover, then learns the friend's grandmother was in the hospital.

facts.fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
facts.hook: Midway through making up, one friend says 'So you felt I picked her over you?' and the other finally relaxes.

facts.fact: The Thomas-Kilmann model, published in 1974, names five ways people handle conflict: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating.
facts.hook: Two friends fighting over a shared project realize one has been avoiding the problem while the other has been competing to win it.

facts.fact: In a 2002 study by Brad Bushman, angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them ended up angrier, not calmer.
facts.hook: After a fight, a student punches a pillow while replaying the argument and notices they feel worse, not better.

facts.fact: A 2016 Ohio State University study of apologies found that the most effective part was acknowledging responsibility, meaning clearly saying that the mistake was your fault.
facts.hook: A kid's first apology text full of excuses gets no reply; the second one says 'That was my fault' and gets an answer.

facts.fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
facts.hook: A friend reads 'sorry if you got upset' aloud and says it sounds like it is her fault for being upset.

facts.fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
facts.hook: A student is sure a friend bumped their tray on purpose, until the friend shows the slippery spot on the floor.

facts.fact: When a person gets angry, the body releases adrenaline, which speeds up heart rate and breathing; this is one reason many people argue less harshly after taking time to calm down.
facts.hook: With a racing heart during a fight at the park, a kid says 'Can we talk tomorrow?' instead of shouting.

facts.fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
facts.hook: A student rewrites 'You never keep secrets' into 'You told Sam what I said on Friday' before talking to a friend.

facts.fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
facts.hook: Two friends who drifted apart after joining different teams find something new they both care about.

facts.fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
facts.hook: A kid tells a parent they have forgiven a friend but are not ready to be best friends again yet, and wonders if that is allowed.

facts.fact: The American Red Cross runs babysitter training courses for young people aged about 11 to 16 that teach child care, safety and how to respond in emergencies.
facts.hook: Before accepting a first babysitting job, a twelve-year-old signs up for a weekend training course at the community center.

facts.fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
facts.hook: A new babysitter reaches for a fluffy blanket for the crib, then remembers the parents' note about safe sleep.

facts.fact: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises cutting grapes into quarters for children under four, because a whole grape is the right size and shape to block a small child's airway.
facts.hook: Making a snack for a three-year-old, a babysitter stops and cuts the grapes into small pieces before serving them.

facts.fact: A swallowed button battery can burn through a child's throat in as little as two hours, so a child who may have swallowed one needs emergency care right away.
facts.hook: A babysitter finds an open remote control with its tiny battery missing and calls the parents and emergency help immediately.

facts.fact: Honey should not be given to babies under 12 months old, because it can contain bacteria spores that grow in an infant's gut and cause a serious illness called infant botulism.
facts.hook: A babysitter almost sweetens a baby's food with honey until an older sibling points to the parents' written instructions.

facts.fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
facts.hook: A babysitter finds a toddler holding an open bottle of cleaner and finds the poison helpline number taped to the fridge.

facts.fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
facts.hook: Frustrated by a baby who will not stop crying, a babysitter puts the baby safely in the crib and steps away for a moment to calm down.

facts.fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
facts.hook: The phone rings during a toddler's bath and the babysitter wraps the child in a towel and brings them along instead of leaving.

facts.fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
facts.hook: Before the parents leave, a babysitter asks for the street address and writes it next to the phone, just in case.

facts.fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
facts.hook: A baby screams as the parents walk out, and the babysitter learns the crying usually fades once a fun distraction begins.

facts.fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
facts.hook: After a messy diaper change, a babysitter hums a song twice at the sink before starting the child's lunch.

facts.fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
facts.hook: A babysitter notices vitamins left on a low coffee table and moves them to a high shelf before the toddler toddles over.

facts.fact: More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause.
facts.hook: Home sick, a student wonders why there is no single cold vaccine and looks up how many viruses cause colds.

facts.fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
facts.hook: A kid complaining about their third cold since fall learns that is pretty normal for their age.

facts.fact: Cold symptoms usually last about 7 to 10 days and go away on their own, since there is no cure for the cold itself.
facts.hook: On day four of a cold, a student worries it will never end, and a pharmacist explains how long colds usually last.

facts.fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
facts.hook: A kid asks the doctor for antibiotics to get back to school faster and learns why they would not work.

facts.fact: People with the flu can spread it starting about one day before they feel any symptoms.
facts.hook: A student realizes they may have caught the flu from a friend who seemed perfectly healthy at the sleepover.

facts.fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
facts.hook: Feeling a little better on day two, a student wants to go to a party, and a parent explains why staying home still matters.

facts.fact: Prescription flu antiviral medicines work best when started within two days after symptoms begin, which is one reason to see a doctor early.
facts.hook: A family debates waiting out a sudden high fever until the weekend, then decides to call the doctor that day.

facts.fact: In a 2015 study, adults who slept less than six hours a night were about four times more likely to catch a cold after being exposed to a cold virus.
facts.hook: A student who has been gaming past midnight all week wakes up with a sore throat and connects the dots.

facts.fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
facts.hook: A kid panics at green tissues, sure they need medicine, and the pharmacist explains what the color really means.

facts.fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
facts.hook: Looking for a pain reliever in the cabinet, a teen checks the label and asks an adult why the aspirin is off-limits.

facts.fact: Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses, which is one reason washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone.
facts.hook: A younger sibling asks why they cannot just rinse with water, and the recovering older kid explains what soap does to the virus.

facts.fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
facts.hook: Blowing their nose again and again with no relief, a student learns why their nose still feels blocked.

facts.fact: In her 1969 book 'On Death and Dying', psychiatrist Elisabeth Kubler-Ross described five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.
facts.hook: After a grandparent's funeral, a student finds a poster listing five stages of grief in the school counselor's office.

facts.fact: Kubler-Ross first described her five stages in people who were themselves dying, and she noted that people do not necessarily go through the stages in a set order.
facts.hook: A kid worries they are grieving wrong because they feel angry after feeling calm, and learns the stages have no fixed order.

facts.fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
facts.hook: A student feels guilty for laughing at a movie the week after a grandparent died, until a parent explains this back-and-forth.

facts.fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
facts.hook: A kid starts wearing their grandfather's old watch and wonders if that means they are not moving on.

facts.fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
facts.hook: Visiting a friend's family during shiva, a student is unsure what to say and learns that simply being there is the point.

facts.fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
facts.hook: A student helps set their late grandmother's photo on an ofrenda and scatters marigold petals toward it.

facts.fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
facts.hook: On the first Qingming since their grandfather died, a kid sweeps his gravestone with cousins and hears stories about him.

facts.fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
facts.hook: A student visiting relatives in Japan helps light a lantern for a grandparent during their first Obon without her.

facts.fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
facts.hook: A student is asked to say a few words at a grandparent's funeral and tries to pick one favorite memory to share.

facts.fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
facts.hook: A kid cannot sleep or eat much the week after a grandmother dies and worries they are getting sick.

facts.fact: Strong feelings of grief often return around birthdays, holidays and the anniversary of a death, which is sometimes called an anniversary reaction.
facts.hook: Months after a grandparent's death, a student feels unexpectedly sad on what would have been his birthday.

facts.fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
facts.hook: Reading a grandparent's obituary, a kid learns he once worked as a sailor, something he had never mentioned.

facts.fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
facts.hook: A skater tries to catch a fall with their hand and ends up at the emergency room with a sore, swollen wrist.

facts.fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
facts.hook: Looking at their X-ray, a kid asks the doctor which of the two bones is the broken one.

facts.fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
facts.hook: A student is surprised to hear their arm is only 'partly' broken and asks what a greenstick fracture means.

facts.fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
facts.hook: At a follow-up visit, the doctor points to a fuzzy lump on the new X-ray and explains it means the bone is healing.

facts.fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
facts.hook: A kid and their grandfather compare casts and wonder why the grandfather's will stay on much longer.

facts.fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
facts.hook: A student staring at their X-ray asks why the bones glow white while their skin is barely visible.

facts.fact: German physicist Wilhelm Rontgen discovered X-rays on November 8, 1895, and weeks later took an X-ray image of his wife's hand.
facts.hook: Waiting for their own X-ray, a kid reads a poster in the hallway about the first X-ray picture ever taken.

facts.fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
facts.hook: A doctor tells a family that the break missed the growth plate, and the kid asks why that is good news.

facts.fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
facts.hook: Choosing a cast color, a student asks how people kept broken bones still before modern casts.

facts.fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
facts.hook: A kid panics as the loud cast saw approaches, and the nurse explains why it will not cut their arm.

facts.fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
facts.hook: Driven crazy by an itch under the cast, a student reaches for a ruler, then remembers the doctor's warning.

facts.fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
facts.hook: When the cast is removed, a kid is shocked at how skinny and weak their arm looks compared to the other one.

facts.fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
facts.hook: An uncle at a family gathering insists a bracelet cured his back pain, and a teen asks what else might explain it.

facts.fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
facts.hook: Testing whether a plant fertilizer works, a student realizes they need an identical pot with no fertilizer.

facts.fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
facts.hook: A friend swears a new energy drink made them run faster, and a student wonders if believing it did the work.

facts.fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
facts.hook: Planning a taste test for a science fair, a student makes sure even the person serving the samples doesn't know which is which.

facts.fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
facts.hook: A student wonders why a study didn't just let volunteers pick whether to try the new medicine.

facts.fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
facts.hook: Reading a headline that links a food to good grades, a student asks what else those students might have in common.

facts.fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
facts.hook: A kid's survey of three friends says everyone loves a snack; the class survey of 200 says something different.

facts.fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
facts.hook: Comparing a blog post and a journal article at the library, a student learns only one was checked by other scientists.

facts.fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
facts.hook: A grandparent credits a new tea for ending a terrible headache, and a teen wonders if it would have eased anyway.

facts.fact: In 1747, Scottish naval surgeon James Lind tested six treatments on twelve sailors with scurvy, and the two given oranges and lemons recovered best, in one of the earliest controlled trials.
facts.hook: A student preparing a report on the history of medicine is amazed that a test on a ship helped prove what cures scurvy.

facts.fact: A 1998 paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism studied only 12 children, was retracted by the journal The Lancet in 2010, and later large studies found no link.
facts.hook: A relative shares an old article at a family dinner, and a teen looks up what happened to the study behind it.

facts.fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
facts.hook: After hearing one vivid story about a shark attack, a kid refuses to swim, then checks how rare attacks really are.

facts.fact: The first national spelling bee in the United States was held in 1925 and won by Frank Neuhauser, who spelled the word 'gladiolus'.
facts.hook: Nervous before the school bee, a student reads about the very first national champion and the flower word he spelled.

facts.fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
facts.hook: Stuck on an unfamiliar word, a speller remembers to ask for its language of origin before starting.

facts.fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
facts.hook: Halfway through a word, a speller realizes a mistake and knows they cannot quietly swap a letter they've already said.

facts.fact: The 'bee' in spelling bee comes from an old word for a gathering of neighbors to help each other, as in a quilting bee or a husking bee.
facts.hook: A younger sibling asks what insects have to do with spelling, and the older one looks up the answer.

facts.fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
facts.hook: Frustrated that 'bite' has a silent e, a student practicing for the bee learns why English spelling is so odd.

facts.fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
facts.hook: Browsing the library before a spelling bee, a student finds a copy of an old dictionary and wonders who decided spellings.

facts.fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
facts.hook: A speller with a cousin in Canada argues over whether 'colour' is wrong, and they look up where the difference began.

facts.fact: The 45-letter word 'pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis' was invented in 1935 by Everett M. Smith, president of the National Puzzlers' League.
facts.hook: Spellers practicing at home dare each other to spell the longest dictionary word and then learn it was made up on purpose.

facts.fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
facts.hook: A speller worried about coming second learns that one national bee ended with eight winners sharing the title.

facts.fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.
facts.hook: At the library, a student preparing for the regional bee reads about recent champions and finds one to look up to.

facts.fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
facts.hook: Instead of rereading the word list again, a speller has a parent quiz them out loud every night.

facts.fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
facts.hook: Hearing 'Greek' as the language of origin, a speller guesses the 'k' sound is spelled 'ch' and gets it right.

facts.fact: The browning of foods like toast and seared meat is mostly the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars, first described by French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard in 1912.
facts.hook: Making grilled cheese for the family, a student wonders why the bread turns golden and tastes so different.

facts.fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
facts.hook: Making caramel for dessert, a kid asks whether it is the same browning as the crust on the roast.

facts.fact: Baking soda, or sodium bicarbonate, only makes a batter rise when it reacts with an acid such as buttermilk, yogurt or lemon juice, producing carbon dioxide bubbles.
facts.hook: Pancakes come out flat after a student swaps buttermilk for plain milk without changing anything else.

facts.fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
facts.hook: Out of baking powder, a kid tries to use baking soda instead and learns why the recipe needs a change.

facts.fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
facts.hook: A student's bread dough doesn't rise, and they realize the water they added was too hot for the yeast.

facts.fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
facts.hook: Baking bread with a grandparent, a kid learns why the dough needs ten minutes of kneading before it rises.

facts.fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
facts.hook: Cooking chicken for dinner, a student checks it with a thermometer instead of guessing from the color.

facts.fact: Bacteria grow fastest between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, so U.S. food safety guidelines say perishable food should not sit at room temperature for more than two hours.
facts.hook: After a family meal, a kid remembers the leftovers are still on the counter hours later and asks if they are safe.

facts.fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
facts.hook: About to chop lettuce on the board they just used for raw chicken, a student grabs a clean one instead.

facts.fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
facts.hook: Frying with a parent nearby, a kid watches the adult slide a lid over a flaring pan instead of reaching for water.

facts.fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects; weighing flour is more accurate.
facts.hook: A student's cookies come out dry and cakey, and a grandparent shows them how to measure flour properly.

facts.fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
facts.hook: Chopping onions for soup, a kid starts crying and asks why a vegetable can make people tear up.

facts.fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
facts.hook: Meeting a Japanese exchange student's grandparents, a kid is unsure how deeply to bow back.

facts.fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
facts.hook: At a friend's house, a student sticks chopsticks into their rice to free a hand, and the friend gently explains why that's avoided.

facts.fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
facts.hook: Riding an elevator in a friend's apartment building, a kid notices there's no button for the fourth floor.

facts.fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
facts.hook: A student picking a housewarming gift for a Chinese family's new home decides against the clock they almost bought.

facts.fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
facts.hook: At a cultural festival, a kid almost ruffles a younger child's hair, and their Thai friend explains the custom.

facts.fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
facts.hook: A student at a friend's family dinner is about to pass a dish with their left hand and notices everyone using their right.

facts.fact: The Thai greeting called the wai is made by pressing the palms together at the chest and bowing slightly.
facts.hook: A student greeting a Thai neighbor's grandmother tries a handshake, and the family shows them the wai instead.

facts.fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
facts.hook: Visiting French cousins, a kid gets confused when one relative gives two cheek kisses and another gives three.

facts.fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
facts.hook: At a school welcome ceremony, a new student from abroad is greeted with a hongi and asks what it means.

facts.fact: Tipping is not customary in Japan, where service charges are usually included in the price.
facts.hook: A family traveling in Japan leaves extra coins on the table, and the server runs after them to return the money.

facts.fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
facts.hook: Eating ramen with a Japanese friend's family, a student is surprised when everyone slurps loudly.

facts.fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
facts.hook: Arriving at a friend's house, a kid notices a row of shoes by the door and a pair of slippers waiting for them.

facts.fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
facts.hook: A kid types 'WHERE ARE YOU' in the group chat just to be noticed, and a friend replies 'why are you yelling?'

facts.fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
facts.hook: After a joke in a chat gets taken seriously, a student learns emoticons were invented for exactly that problem.

facts.fact: The first widely used emoji set, 176 small pictures drawn on a 12-by-12 pixel grid, was designed by Shigetaka Kurita for the Japanese phone company NTT DoCoMo around 1999.
facts.hook: Arguing over what an emoji means, two friends look up where emoji came from in the first place.

facts.fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
facts.hook: A kid wonders why their friend thinks 'Okay.' sounds angry while 'okay' sounds fine.

facts.fact: A 2005 study led by psychologist Justin Kruger found that people sending emails greatly overestimated how well readers could tell whether a message was sarcastic or serious.
facts.hook: A sarcastic comment in a group chat gets taken as an insult, and the sender can't understand why nobody got the joke.

facts.fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
facts.hook: Setting rules for a new class group chat, a student looks up whether anyone ever wrote official online manners.

facts.fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
facts.hook: An eleven-year-old trying to sign up for a social app wonders why it keeps asking for their birthday.

facts.fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
facts.hook: A student is shocked by a mean comment from a classmate who is always polite in person.

facts.fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
facts.hook: A kid deletes an embarrassing public post and later learns an old copy may still exist.

facts.fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
facts.hook: Sending a party invitation email to the whole class, a student uses BCC so nobody's address gets shared with everyone.

facts.fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
facts.hook: A kid's private message complaining about a friend turns up as a screenshot in a different group chat.

facts.fact: Engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between separate computers in 1971 and chose the @ symbol to separate a user's name from the computer's name.
facts.hook: Setting up their first email address, a student wonders why every address has an @ in the middle.
